passage: The morning bus from the village to the kasba school was always packed. Tushar sat near the back, as usual, while a group of older boys copied the way he stammered on his name. Some girls giggled. Urmila, squeezed by the window with her tiffin on her lap, felt her face go hot. Her cousin was among the boys. If she said anything, it would reach every house in the village by evening. The bus jolted past the sugarcane fields. Tushar stared at his knees. Urmila stood up, walked down the swaying aisle and sat beside him. "Enough," she said loudly. "Would you like it done to you?" Her cousin rolled his eyes and muttered something. The boys went quiet, a little sulky. Tushar didn't say a word, but he moved his bag so she had room.

qa.q: Where was the bus going?
qa.a: It was going from the village to the kasba school.

qa.q: Why did Urmila hesitate before speaking up?
qa.a: She feared the social cost, since her cousin was one of the teasers and gossip would spread through the village by evening.

qa.q: How could a teacher support what Urmila started?
qa.a: A teacher could quietly check in with Tushar, speak to the older boys about the teasing, and back Urmila so she isn't left facing the backlash alone.

qa.q: How might Tushar have experienced Urmila sitting beside him?
qa.a: After feeling humiliated, he probably felt less alone and protected; moving his bag suggests quiet gratitude.

grounding: A teen in a small-town setting defends a teased peer even though it risks trouble with her own cousin and neighbours.

passage: In the cafeteria of a high school in Toronto, Soo-ah opened her lunch box of kimbap, and a boy at the next table held his nose and laughed. His friends joined in. Camila, who usually sat with the popular crowd by the windows, watched Soo-ah quietly close the lid. Camila's stomach turned. She picked up her tray, walked across the room and sat opposite Soo-ah. "That looks amazing. Can I try one? I'll trade you my crackers." Soo-ah blinked, then slid the box over. The window table went silent, then someone snorted. Over the next week, Camila wasn't invited to a birthday party she'd assumed she'd be at. It stung. But she kept sitting with Soo-ah, and by Friday two others had joined them.

qa.q: What did Camila offer Soo-ah in exchange?
qa.a: She offered to trade her crackers for one of the kimbap.

qa.q: What does Camila's turning stomach suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She was upset and uncomfortable watching Soo-ah being mocked, which pushed her to act.

qa.q: What did it cost Camila to stand by Soo-ah, and why was it still worth it?
qa.a: She lost an invitation to a party and some status, but she stayed loyal to what felt right and it gave Soo-ah company.

qa.q: How might the popular group see Camila's choice?
qa.a: Some may feel embarrassed or annoyed at being shown up, which could explain the snort and the missing invitation.

grounding: Shows a teen defending a mocked peer at a social cost and sticking with that choice.

passage: In the school bus queue, three boys from the cricket team had surrounded Sachin again. 'S-s-sachin, s-say your name,' one of them sang, and the others laughed. Farida, fifteen, felt her stomach drop. Those boys were friends with everyone she wanted to be friends with. She had watched this happen twice already and said nothing. This time she stepped out of the line. 'Stop it. It's not funny.' Her voice came out smaller than she wanted. One of them rolled his eyes. 'Relax, it's a joke.' 'Then laugh at yourselves.' She stood beside Sachin until the bus came. On board, a girl she barely knew moved her bag so Farida could sit. Later that week Farida heard she was being called 'the preachy one.' She told the class teacher what had happened anyway.

qa.q: How many times had Farida watched this happen before?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why did Farida's stomach drop before she spoke?
qa.a: She was afraid of losing standing, since the boys were friends with people she wanted to be close to.

qa.q: Why was Farida's later step, telling the teacher, important?
qa.a: It brought in an adult who can stop the bullying for Sachin, instead of leaving it to one brave moment.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt when Farida stood beside him?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone, though maybe also embarrassed to be the centre of attention. 🤍

grounding: Shows a teenager defending a bullied classmate despite the social cost, then involving a teacher.

passage:
Dear Lalit,
I know you're angry that I showed the group chat to Ma'am. I'm writing because you won't pick up my calls. I didn't do it to get you in trouble. When the edited photos of the new boy started, I laughed at the first one. Then someone wrote that he should just leave the school. He's been absent three days since. I kept thinking, what if that was my little brother? I know everyone's calling me a snitch. Two people have left me on read all week. It's awful, honestly. But I'd rather lose some friends than watch someone get pushed out. You were never one of the people making them. I hope you'll talk to me.
Kashish

qa.q: How many days has the new boy been absent?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What does Kashish mean by 'It's awful, honestly'?
qa.a: Kashish is hurt by being called a snitch and ignored, so the social cost weighs heavily even though Kashish stands by the choice.

qa.q: What could Kashish do if the teasing of Kashish continues?
qa.a: Tell a teacher or parent and lean on supportive friends, while staying calm and not hitting back.

qa.q: How might Lalit see this letter?
qa.a: Lalit may still be angry but could soften, since Kashish says Lalit wasn't one of those making the photos and wants to stay friends.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager reporting online bullying of a classmate and bearing the unpopularity that followed.

passage: Sachin, thanks for having me on the school podcast. So, I'm Jatin, Class 11. Last month, in the canteen, some seniors were mocking a boy for his lunch, calling it smelly, filming him. Everyone laughed or looked away. I nearly did too. Then I thought about my little brother, and I walked over, sat next to the boy and said, 'Smells great, actually. Can I try?' The seniors turned on me. Someone called me a loser. That afternoon I went with the boy to our class teacher and told her what happened and about the video. She called the seniors in the same day. People still tease me a bit. I'd do it again.

qa.q: What were the seniors doing to the boy?
qa.a: Mocking him for his lunch, calling it smelly and filming him.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he decided to walk over?
qa.a: Jatin felt nervous but protective, unwilling to join the crowd against the boy.

qa.q: What made Jatin's response effective?
qa.a: Jatin supported the boy on the spot and, the same day, took the matter to the class teacher with the boy.

qa.q: How might the bullied boy have felt when Jatin sat beside him?
qa.a: Relieved and less alone, finally with someone on his side.

grounding: Shows a teenager standing up for a bullied peer despite social risk and getting adult help the same day.

passage: I'm Maria, and I sit near Farhan in Class 10. Last week someone posted an edited photo of a new boy in our class group, with a cruel caption. Messages flew. Laughing emojis everywhere. Farhan, fifteen, typed: "This isn't funny. Delete it." For a minute nobody replied. Then someone wrote, "Chill, bro," and a few people left the group. Farhan didn't back down. At lunch he went to our class teacher with a screenshot, and the photo was gone by the evening. I don't know if he was scared, but I saw his hands shake while he typed.

qa.q: What did Farhan type in the class group?
qa.a: "This isn't funny. Delete it."

qa.q: What might Farhan have felt as his hands shook while typing?
qa.a: He was probably nervous but determined, knowing speaking up was risky.

qa.q: What made Farhan's actions effective?
qa.a: He spoke up in the group and took the screenshot to the teacher the same day.

qa.q: How does Maria see Farhan's courage?
qa.a: Maria noticed his shaking hands and seems to respect that he spoke up anyway.

grounding: Shows a teenager standing up for a peer targeted online despite social risk, seen by a classmate.

passage: Monday: a new girl, Sabina, joined Class 9, and some girls started whispering about her clothes. Ritu, fourteen, noticed but stayed quiet, afraid she'd be next. Wednesday: the whispers turned into a nickname, shouted across the corridor. Sabina ate lunch alone. Ritu's stomach twisted. She picked up her tiffin and sat with Sabina. "Mind if I sit here?" That afternoon Ritu went to her class teacher and told her about the nickname; the teacher spoke to the girls before the last bell. Friday: two other girls joined their table. The nickname faded, though Ritu lost one friend over it.

qa.q: What did the girls whisper about?
qa.a: Sabina's clothes.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when her stomach twisted?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy watching Sabina eat alone, torn between fear and doing what was right.

qa.q: Which choices by Ritu made a difference?
qa.a: Sitting with Sabina and telling the class teacher the same afternoon, so an adult acted quickly.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt when Ritu sat down?
qa.a: Relieved and less alone, after days of isolation.

grounding: Shows a teenager moving from silence to standing up for a bullied peer, despite the social cost.

passage: Preeti Maasi tapped Arohi's hand. "When I was fifteen, a new girl, Kamla, joined our class from a village near Bikaner. She spoke with a thick accent, and the popular girls copied it every time she answered. Everyone laughed, even me, the first week. One day they took her notebook and read out her spelling mistakes. I felt sick. I stood up and said, 'Give it back. That's enough.' My hands were shaking. The room went dead quiet. Then I told our class teacher at lunch, and she spoke to the whole class that afternoon. The popular girls didn't talk to me for two months. But Kamla sat with me after that, and she became my closest friend." Arohi asked, "Were you scared?" "Very. I still did it."

qa.q: Where did Kamla come from?
qa.a: A village near Bikaner.

qa.q: How did young Preeti feel when she stood up?
qa.a: She felt scared, hands shaking, but sickened enough by the bullying to act.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Preeti's story, and what did she do after standing up?
qa.a: Deciding to stop laughing and say "That's enough"; she then told the class teacher at lunch.

qa.q: How might Kamla have felt when Preeti stood up for her?
qa.a: Kamla likely felt relieved and less alone, which is why they became close friends.

grounding: An aunt remembers standing up for a bullied classmate at fifteen, at a social cost.

passage: The school bus was crammed and noisy after the Friday match, and the teacher on duty was sitting up front. At the back, two seniors had taken Jaya's bag, a Class 8 student, and were tossing it over her head while she tried to grab it. "Come on, jump!" People laughed. Eshaan, sixteen, felt his stomach tighten. These were his cricket friends. If he said something, they'd call him soft. Jaya's face was turning red, and she was close to tears. Eshaan stood up. "Give it back. Now." One of them snorted. "Relax, man." "Now." He held out his hand. After a pause, they tossed it to him, and he gave it to Jaya. Then he walked to the front, the bus lurching, and told the teacher what had happened. She went straight to the back.

qa.q: When was the bus crammed and noisy?
qa.a: After the Friday match.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when his stomach tightened?
qa.a: He felt torn and anxious, afraid of how his friends would react, but uncomfortable watching Jaya upset.

qa.q: Which two things did Eshaan do, and why do both matter?
qa.a: He got the bag back and told the teacher on duty, so Jaya was helped right away and an adult could deal with the seniors.

qa.q: How might Jaya have experienced the ride?
qa.a: She likely felt humiliated and frightened, then relieved when Eshaan stepped in.

grounding: On a crowded bus, a teenager stands up to his friends to defend a younger student and tells the teacher.

passage: At the Dadar coaching centre, a group of boys in the back row started imitating Pallavi's stammer whenever she answered. "W-w-well, Sir..." Some girls giggled. Urmila, sixteen, sat two rows away. Last week she had laughed along, quietly, and hated herself for it. Today Pallavi went silent halfway through an answer, her ears red. Urmila turned around. "Stop it. It's not funny." The boys rolled their eyes. "Chill, it's a joke." "It's not," Urmila said, louder, her voice shaking. The room went quiet. At the break, she sat next to Pallavi, and after class, she told the centre head exactly what had happened. The head called the boys in that evening. On the way out, Pallavi squeezed Urmila's hand without saying anything.

qa.q: What were the boys imitating?
qa.a: Pallavi's stammer.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when her voice shook?
qa.a: She felt nervous and scared, but also angry and ashamed of having laughed before.

qa.q: What did Urmila do after standing up to the boys, and why was it important?
qa.a: She sat with Pallavi and told the centre head the same day, so an adult could stop the bullying.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when Urmila spoke up?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and grateful, shown by her silent hand squeeze. 🤍

grounding: A teenager defends a classmate mocked for her stammer and reports it, despite the social risk.

"Why are you sitting with Kirti? Everyone's laughing at you," Tenzin whispered at the Class 9 lunch table.
"Everyone's laughing at her," Sarita said. "That's why."
"They're making a video of her eating. You'll end up in it."
Sarita stood up, walked to the boys with the phone, and said, loudly enough for three tables to hear, "Delete it. That's not funny."
"Relax, it's a joke."

Tenzin hissed, "Now they'll hate you."

After lunch, she did. The class teacher called the boys in that same afternoon and spoke to Kirti's parents by evening.

passage:
I still remember the poll someone posted in our class chat one night: "Who is the weirdest girl in 11-C?" Manjula's name was winning.
I'm Kashish. I was in the chat. I had voted in silly polls before. This one made my stomach twist, because Manjula had stopped coming to the canteen.
I typed: "This isn't funny, it's cruel. I'm leaving and I'm reporting it." Then I left. Two people called me a snitch in the corridor the next day.
But that same evening I had shown the poll to our class teacher. The next morning it was gone, and the teacher spoke to the class. Manjula came to the canteen again that week.
I lost two friends. I'd do it again.

qa.q: What was the class chat poll asking?
qa.a: "Who is the weirdest girl in 11-C?"

qa.q: How did Kashish feel on seeing the poll?
qa.a: Kashish felt uneasy and sick with worry, because Manjula had stopped coming to the canteen.

qa.q: What made Kashish's approach work?
qa.a: Kashish objected openly and showed the poll to the class teacher the same evening, so an adult acted the next morning.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt on coming back to the canteen?
qa.a: Manjula may have felt a little safer and relieved, though still hurt by the poll.

grounding: A teen recalls calling out an online bullying poll and reporting it despite losing friends.

passage:
Coach's note, Under-16 hockey squad
At Thursday practice, some players kept calling Francis names about his accent and passing around him. Most of the squad laughed along.
Neelam, our vice-captain, stopped the drill. She said, "If we're a team, he's on it. Pass properly or I'll take it to Coach." A couple of seniors rolled their eyes at her. She kept her stick down until they started passing to him.
After practice she came to me and told me what had been happening for two weeks. I spoke to Francis privately that evening; he said he had been thinking of quitting. I have talked to the players involved and informed his parents and the sports head.
Neelam lost some popularity with the seniors this week. I told her I noticed, and that it mattered.

qa.q: What were some players mocking Francis about?
qa.a: His accent.

qa.q: How was Francis feeling before Neelam stepped in?
qa.a: He felt left out and hurt, enough that he had been thinking of quitting.

qa.q: What did Neelam do that helped, and what did the coach add?
qa.a: Neelam stopped the drill and reported it; the coach spoke to Francis that evening and informed the players, his parents and the sports head.

qa.q: How might the seniors who rolled their eyes see Neelam now?
qa.a: They may feel annoyed at her, but some may also respect that she held her ground.

grounding: A coach records a teen defending a mocked teammate despite losing popularity.

passage:
Dear Diary, Tuesday
At lunch, Nikhil's group grabbed Vidya's lunchbox again and passed it round, making fun of the smell of her fish curry. Everyone laughed, like always. My face was hot. Nikhil is sort of my friend, and they let me sit with them. But I stood up and said, "Give it back. It's not funny." It went totally quiet. Someone muttered "hero". I took the box and gave it to Vidya. Her hands were shaking. After lunch I went with her to Ms Thomas and told her it happens every week. Ms Thomas thanked us, wrote it down, said she'd speak to Nikhil's group and their parents today, and will check on Vidya first thing tomorrow. Tomorrow I'll probably eat alone. Still glad.
Rafiq

qa.q: What did Nikhil's group make fun of?
qa.a: The smell of Vidya's fish curry.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel standing up to Nikhil's group?
qa.a: Rafiq felt nervous and hot-faced, risking a place at their table, but glad to have done it.

qa.q: What made Rafiq's response more than a one-time rescue?
qa.a: Going with Vidya to Ms Thomas the same day meant an adult could deal with the weekly bullying, not just this lunch.

qa.q: What is it like for Vidya when Rafiq hands back the lunchbox?
qa.a: Vidya is shaken but likely relieved and less alone, seeing someone finally step in. 🤍
